title_en: Microsoft declares ‘Code Red’ after huge Outlook outage
title_fa: Microsoft declares ‘Code Red’ after huge Outlook outage
excerpt_en: This month's Exchange Online and Microsoft Outlook outage has prompted the software giant to declare an unusual "Code Red" internally, Reuters reports. The nearly 24-hour outage took down email for millions of customers, and was triggered by a bug that had been sitting on...
excerpt_fa: This month's Exchange Online and Microsoft Outlook outage has prompted the software giant to declare an unusual "Code Red" internally, Reuters reports. The nearly 24-hour outage took down email for millions of customers, and was triggered by a bug that had been sitting on...
content_en:
This month’s Exchange Online and Microsoft Outlook outage has prompted the software giant to declare an unusual “Code Red” internally, Reuters reports. The nearly 24-hour outage took down email for millions of customers, and was triggered by a bug that had been sitting on Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers since July without any impact to servers.
Microsoft declares ‘Code Red’ after huge Outlook outage
Microsoft is now holding daily meetings with the engineering group responsible for Microsoft 365 services.
Microsoft is now holding daily meetings with the engineering group responsible for Microsoft 365 services.
In a memo to the teams responsible for Exchange Online, Microsoft 365 Core president Jason Henderson revealed the outage was the most significant in history for Microsoft’s customers. “Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday,” said Henderson. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team.”
As part of this Code Red declaration, Microsoft is focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning, and faster recovery mechanisms. Microsoft now has a target of resolving future outages within an hour, and will reportedly deploy AI agents to help engineers diagnose issues. Microsoft is now holding daily meetings with the engineering group responsible for Microsoft 365 services, alongside weekly reviews.
In a separate memo, Amanda Silver, Microsoft’s corporate vice president of M365 Core and Work IQ, said engineers had to work through a “fog of war” to help resolve the outage. I reported last week that Microsoft engineers had a running bridge call during the entire outage, and at one point it hit the maximum of 1,000 participants.
Microsoft engineers had to exchange messages across 11 Teams chats and reportedly “struggled to maintain a cohesive picture” during the outage because of the fragmented internal tracking systems. Sources tell me the outage was marked as “sev0,” the highest level, which indicates a catastrophic level of service disruption. Engineers struggled to get servers back online because they had entered maintenance mode and became unresponsive due to unusually high CPU loads.

title_en: How to watch every 2026 NFL Thanksgiving game on streaming
title_fa: How to watch every 2026 NFL Thanksgiving game on streaming
excerpt_en: Thanksgiving Eve brings a first-ever NFL game, plus three more on Turkey Day. Here's where to stream every matchup in 2026 without missing a snap.
excerpt_fa: Thanksgiving Eve brings a first-ever NFL game, plus three more on Turkey Day. Here's where to stream every matchup in 2026 without missing a snap.
content_en:
How to watch every 2026 NFL Thanksgiving game on streaming
Cutting cable should never stop a tradition.
Death, taxes and vegging out on the couch to watch Thanksgiving football are three givens in America. This year's holiday slate is jam-packed with major storylines, including division rivals, star players, big-name halftime performers and, for the first time, an extra matchup on Thanksgiving Eve.
With games spread across both streaming services and TV networks, knowing how, where and when to stream the NFL has become a sport of its own, but we've got you covered.
Where to stream on Thanksgiving Eve
Today, you can stream Packers at Rams exclusively on Netflix, kicking off at 8:15PM ET/5:15PM PT. If you don't have an active subscription, you can sign up for the ad-supported tier at $8.99/month. Signing up today will also get you access to this year's Christmas Day games.
Since this is the NFL's first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game, the league is bringing out a big name for halftime: U2 will perform at SoFi Stadium fresh off the release of its new album, Carnaval De Luz. Unlike 2014's Songs of Innocence, it didn't show up on your iPhone overnight, so you may have missed it.
Where to stream on Thanksgiving
On Turkey Day itself, the action kicks off at 1PM ET/10AM PT with Bears at Lions, airing on CBS and streaming on Paramount+. You can get Paramount+ starting at $8.99/month to watch the game and see Wu-Tang Clan swarm the stage for a halftime show executive produced by Michigan-bred icon Eminem.
Next on the docket is Eagles at Cowboys, starting at 4:30PM ET. The game airs live on Fox, but it's the one matchup you can stream at no cost on Tubi. It's also available on the Fox One streaming service for $19.99/month. Texas native Miranda Lambert is set to perform at this year's Salvation Army Red Kettle Kickoff Halftime Show, marking 30 years of the annual tradition.
Then, two of the league's premier quarterbacks, Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen, face off to close out the night with Chiefs at Bills. This matchup airs live on NBC and streams on Peacock at 8:20PM ET. You'll need the Premium tier to watch on Peacock, which starts at $12.99/month. Like the prior game, the NFL tapped a local act, the Goo Goo Dolls, to headline halftime in Buffalo.
If you cut cable a while ago but don't want to sign up for individual subscriptions, you can watch these three NFL games on live TV streaming services, including YouTube TV (starting at $49.99/month for the Sports tier), Hulu + Live TV (starting at $99.99/month) or DIRECTV (starting at $94.99/month). Eagles at Cowboys and Chiefs at Bills will also be available to stream on Sling TV Select ($19.99/month) or a higher tier.
Where to stream on Black Friday
On Black Friday, you can stream Broncos at Steelers on Prime Video at 3PM ET. If you're not a Prime subscriber, you can score a standalone subscription for $8.99/month. This matchup will not feature a halftime performance, but two of the league's top teams should suffice.

title_en: Amazon Autos is coming to the UK in its first expansion outside the US
title_fa: Amazon Autos is coming to the UK in its first expansion outside the US
excerpt_en: Amazon Autos will start selling cars in the UK early next year, marking the first time it has expanded outside the US.
excerpt_fa: Amazon Autos will start selling cars in the UK early next year, marking the first time it has expanded outside the US.
content_en:
Amazon Autos is coming to the UK in its first expansion outside the US
The service will arrive in early 2027 with Hyundai as its first announced launch partner.
Amazon will start selling cars in the UK early next year, marking the first time its Amazon Autos service has expanded outside the US. Buyers will be able to browse new and used models, check financing rates and reserve vehicles, though they'll still need to visit a dealership to complete the transaction. As it was in the US, Hyundai will be the first announced launch partner for the service, along with the UK dealership Vertu Motors, with more automakers and dealers to be announced in the coming months.
"Buying a car is one of the biggest purchases people make, and we think it should feel as simple and transparent as shopping for anything on Amazon," said Amazon Autos International director Matt Nuffort. "We worked closely with UK dealers to design the experience, and they're excited that we're bringing them customers who are ready to buy."
As in the US, shoppers will be able to browse vehicles by make, model, color and price, comparing personal contract purchase, hire purchase and cash options. Amazon is promising "transparent, upfront pricing," instant part exchange (trade-in) estimates and nearby dealer locations. Amazon will effectively act as a storefront, with final sales and financing fully handled by dealerships.
With Amazon Autos in the US, availability of certain brands and models for new and used vehicles varies by region and participating dealerships. The site handles 14 different brands that sell both new and used vehicles, along with 21 other makes that sell used vehicles only, for 35 altogether. The service has expanded stateside from 48 cities at launch to more than 150, and now works with thousands of dealers.
Amazon provides dealers with pre-qualified customers, but it doesn't take a commission on sales. Instead, revenue comes from ad-based subscription fees and advertising, according to an Amazon Autos FAQ page. Earlier this year, Automotive News reported that some US dealers were saying that the e-commerce giant has been "slow to deliver tangible results," to the tune of just one or two sales per month.

title_en: US financial crimes bureau discloses ‘cybersecurity incident’
title_fa: US financial crimes bureau discloses ‘cybersecurity incident’
excerpt_en: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed on Tuesday that it's investigating a "cybersecurity incident." The bureau, which is part of the Treasury Department, said it's looking into an "incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its...
excerpt_fa: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed on Tuesday that it's investigating a "cybersecurity incident." The bureau, which is part of the Treasury Department, said it's looking into an "incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its...
content_en:
The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed on Tuesday that it’s investigating a “cybersecurity incident.” The bureau, which is part of the Treasury Department, said it’s looking into an “incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems.” It hasn’t offered any information about the full scope or source of the breach, but FinCEN has taken some systems offline as a precaution.
US financial crimes bureau discloses ‘cybersecurity incident’
FinCEN’s alert comes in the wake of a reported breach of unclassified information at US spy agencies, including the CIA.
FinCEN’s alert comes in the wake of a reported breach of unclassified information at US spy agencies, including the CIA.
The news comes hours after The New York Times reported that the Central Intelligence Agency and Office of the Director of National Security discovered a breach of an open source intelligence system, exposing unclassified information. The Department of Defense, whose National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency was also reportedly impacted by the breach, declined to comment. The CIA and ODNI did not immediately respond to requests for comment. It’s unclear if the FinCEN breach is related. Americans have been on high alert about security incidents after a series of seemingly unrelated outages earlier this month.
Americans have been on high alert about security incidents
FinCEN’s role is to protect the financial system from illegal activity, including by combatting money laundering and terrorism financing. The bureau maintains financial transaction data and distributes it for law enforcement purposes. FinCEN also houses reports of suspicious activity that financial institutions file as part of the Bank Secrecy Act.
FinCEN says in its alert that banks can still file reports about suspicious activity online, but some services may not be immediately available. Filers that need to expedite their reports in the meantime can still call the Financial Institutions Hotline, which it says was not impacted by the disruption.
Update, November 24th: Added response from Department of Defense.

title_en: Change this Roku TV setting to watch movies how they were filmed
title_fa: Change this Roku TV setting to watch movies how they were filmed
excerpt_en: Your TV's refresh rate might be set to 60fps by default, but you can change that.
excerpt_fa: Your TV's refresh rate might be set to 60fps by default, but you can change that.
content_en:
Change this Roku TV setting to watch movies how they were filmed
You don't have to leave your TV's refresh rate at 60fps.
If you were to travel back in time thirty years and show someone a smart TV from today, their head would likely explode. In addition to the seemingly limitless amount of content one can find and interact with on a modern television, your Roku TV also may have the ability to let you watch movies in a far more compelling way.
Buried deep in your Roku TV's settings is a way to alter the refresh rate, and there's a very specific reason that you might want to do that. Most Roku TVs default to a refresh rate of 60fps. While that's going to be perfectly fine for some situations, it doesn't make for the most theatrical viewing experience — for the most part, movies are filmed and projected at 24fps. It's the standard, and it has defined the way movies look and feel for decades. When you go to the movie theater, you're watching a 24fps output.
Roku allows you to alter your TV's refresh rate to match that, offering something a bit closer to the original intent of those films.
How to change your TV's refresh rate to 24fps to achieve a film look
There are a lot of ways to change the overall look and display of your Roku TV, but most of that discourse seems centered around colors and contrast. Those things are important, but if you really want to achieve a "movie look," then you'll want to change the refresh rate.
In your Roku TV, to match this unique look, you'll need to first go to the main menu. From here, select Settings, and then go into System. In this menu, you'll find something called Advanced System Settings, which will allow you to access Advanced Display Settings. You want to turn Auto-adjust display refresh rate on.
It's a one-click and done solution, as it will self-adjust itself to match the native refresh rate of any movie or TV show you put on. Because films have a native refresh rate of 24fps, your TV will now run them as such. The same goes for TV shows, which may be filmed at 30 or 60fps. It's a tiny adjustment, but it's one that will make your viewing experience even better.

title_en: This helpful Apple Watch feature works seamlessly with Apple CarPlay
title_fa: This helpful Apple Watch feature works seamlessly with Apple CarPlay
excerpt_en: Long drives call for every trick you can get. See how your Apple Watch and CarPlay team up to keep you on course and a little more alert behind the wheel.
excerpt_fa: Long drives call for every trick you can get. See how your Apple Watch and CarPlay team up to keep you on course and a little more alert behind the wheel.
content_en:
This helpful Apple Watch feature works seamlessly with Apple CarPlay
Some drivers swear by this Apple Watch feature, and it's probably already switched on.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
If you're deep into the Apple ecosystem, the choice between Apple Maps and Google Maps isn't as clear-cut as it used to be. The first was initially a disaster, even threatening the lives of Australian drivers due to inaccuracies. Since then, however, Apple has totally overhauled the app, and these days there's often little to no practical difference — speaking as someone who recently drove cross-country to move to a new city.
I did prefer Apple Maps for that drive for one big reason: my Apple Watch. I knew that I'd be driving for hours at a time, and it was essential to exploit anything and everything to stay alert. Linked with CarPlay, the Apple Watch offers a distinct advantage in the form of haptic feedback.
Most likely this option will already be on once you've configured your watch. But you can double-check this on your iPhone and turn off the feature if it becomes more of an annoyance than a benefit.
How your Apple Watch integrates with CarPlay
With haptic feedback active, your Apple Watch taps your wrist whenever a turn is imminent. These vibrations coincide with CarPlay's audio and visual alerts, so it's always clear what you're supposed to do. You can even choose different vibration patterns depending on whether you need to turn left or right. This makes it virtually impossible to miss a turnoff; the feature might even be lifesaving if you're prone to nodding off on long drives.
As mentioned, these alerts should be on by default. If you want to verify that or disable them, open the Watch app on your iPhone. On the My Watch tab, select Apps, then Maps. If you like, you can toggle alerts for Driving with CarPlay, plus any other driving, walking or cycling.
Whether or not you disable CarPlay integration, you'll probably want to leave cycling alerts on. Apple Maps can be handy while riding a bike or a personal electric vehicle such as a scooter or electric unicycle, but it's sometimes difficult to check your screen and ride at the same time. Audio and haptics may be your only practical cues to make a turn.
Can you drive with just your Apple Watch?
Unfortunately, it's impossible to run CarPlay exclusively from your Apple Watch. Even the Apple Watch Ultra 4 lacks the necessary horsepower, and CarPlay would be an immense battery drain regardless. Since Apple Watches also lack USB ports, they'd be restricted to wireless CarPlay at best.
You can get driving directions directly from the watchOS version of Apple Maps. You'll get the same sort of haptics we've been talking about, plus audio and visual guidance. If you don't have your iPhone, you'll need to download offline maps or use a watch with an active cellular plan. Many carriers charge extra for smartwatch coverage, even though you're rarely going to use your watch and phone data at the same time.
While you can get Google Maps on an Apple Watch, directions won't work without your iPhone. There's no watchOS option for offline maps, and Apple Watches are largely restricted to first-party apps while on cellular. These issues may be solved someday, but neither Apple nor Google seems that eager to tackle them.

content_en:
Investors cheered Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s CEO on Monday, but renowned business academic Jeffrey Sonnenfeld of Yale thinks they’re celebrating a mistake. He sees a company that is largely responsible for putting sophisticated technology in the hands of the country’s adversaries, at a moment when the risks couldn’t be higher. Far from a champion of American industry, he says, Nvidia is “a detriment to U.S. global industrial might.”
As evidence, Sonnenfeld points to research suggesting Nvidia’s most advanced chips have reached China despite U.S. export controls and to sinking shares of Anthropic, which he links to the realization that China’s seemingly miraculous open source AI models are, in a sense, copies of top U.S. labs’ work, even as Nvidia has insisted that smuggling is a “non-factor.”
Indeed, Huang’s return was greeted with just as much enthusiasm in Asia, The Washington Post reported. “The king is back!” read one headline from China’s state-affiliated Star Market Daily.
The reinstatement itself followed heavy pressure from Washington. Nvidia’s chairman had effectively ruled out Huang’s return just last week. Then, in a torrent of private weekend calls led by Vice President JD Vance, top administration officials leaned on the board to welcome Huang back, with President Trump calling the board directly to vouch for him. “I made the deal,” Trump told CNBC on Monday.
Sonnenfeld says the directors who went along, and who returned Huang to the board even as it investigates whether foreign intelligence efforts targeted him, now face a “historic level of individual liability.”
The legal deluge has already begun. As we noted a couple of weeks ago, a potential class-action lawsuit was filed almost immediately. Days later, a shareholder derivative suit followed. Filed on Nvidia’s behalf against the directors themselves, the suit alleges the board ignored red flags about Huang’s relationship with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang.
The class action is very much aimed at making Nvidia and Huang compensate investors for their losses, while the derivative suit puts the directors’ own behavior on trial, with any recovery going to Nvidia. Three more suits followed on November 18, the day after Nvidia’s most recent earnings call; all five were filed in Northern California, where Nvidia is based.
Huang and Nvidia are also juggling a Justice Department antitrust investigation, a reported SEC probe into Nvidia’s accounting, a possible FBI review, a California subpoena, an export-control case that landed partner Megaspeed on the U.S. trade blacklist on Monday, and congressional inquiries, including a Senate Banking hearing next week at which Huang has agreed to testify.
Here’s more of what Sonnenfeld had to say, in a Q&A that’s been edited for length and clarity.
So much has happened since we last talked. Huang was ousted, he’s come back. Do you think the board’s reliance on government assurances here is defensible or an abdication of its own duties?
They failed to rely on experts. That’s one of the reasons this board is going to be sued and lose, and these directors are likely to face a historic level of individual liability. They have a very inadequate directors and officers liability policy. They have also just failed in their diligence. They hired the Wachtell [law] firm. The Wachtell firm barely got off the blocks to do an investigation. And then they have already reversed themselves, so they didn’t use the expertise needed.
It’s wild that they also put Huang right back on the board of directors.
The board showed, in addition to incompetence and collaboration, just cowardice in their capitulation because Trump has nothing to wave over them. If this was SpaceX, where 46% of its business comes from the government [you could maybe see the case for Trump’s involvement]. For Nvidia, it’s not even 1% of its business that comes from the U.S. government, so [the board] didn’t have that threat. [Trump] can call off [federal] investigations, but he can’t call off the shareholder litigation. Some are already filed, and the estimates are there’ll probably be 30 of them, and they’re going to be extremely costly.
And this is not, by the way, just a blue or red state issue. We already have 14 GOP senators who’ve already come out against this, and very prominent conservatives, like Pete Ricketts and Josh Hawley and Tom Cotton and John Cornyn. Those are some issues that may help explain why Nvidia’s stock is tumbling today.
Might the board say, “We saw the classified intelligence findings, and they assure us Jensen will be absolved of wrongdoing”?
They haven’t seen those findings, and we also haven’t seen what will be the result of the Senate Intelligence Committee, the Senate Special Committee on Investigations, the Senate Banking Committee, and all their House counterparts. The board hasn’t seen any of that, and even if they saw it, which they have not yet, that still wouldn’t matter.
Do you think the Commerce Department will continue to tighten its chip export controls to keep China from accessing so much compute or walk back some of those recent moves?
We already see that Megaspeed has finally been put on the sanctions list, as it should have been before. And we have documentation now that Nvidia, rather than a champion of U.S. global industrial might, is actually a detriment to U.S. global industrial might, because their chips have now turned out to be in the hands and in the systems of not just the Chinese military, as they got channeled to Northwestern Polytechnical University, which is a military institution — this is going into weapons that will, of course, be funneled to Iran and Russia, and they didn’t have access to that a year ago. title_en: Trump reportedly says pardoning Jensen Huang is ‘an option’
title_fa: Trump reportedly says pardoning Jensen Huang is ‘an option’
excerpt_en: Huang faces ongoing questions about his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive with alleged ties to Chinese intelligence who previously worked for a company that has been accused of illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China.
excerpt_fa: Huang faces ongoing questions about his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive with alleged ties to Chinese intelligence who previously worked for a company that has been accused of illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China.
content_en:
During an interview with the New York Post on Tuesday, President Trump said that pardoning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has been ensnared in a scandal involving an alleged Chinese spy, is “an option,” albeit one that he doesn’t think he will have to exercise.
“It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary,” the president reportedly told the outlet.
Huang, who was ousted from his own company less than two weeks ago, was reinstated Monday. He faces ongoing questions about his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive with alleged ties to Chinese intelligence who previously worked for a company that has been accused of illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China.
Huang is scheduled to testify at a public Senate Banking Committee hearing next week.
When asked about the hearing, Trump reportedly said: “I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know a very smart person.”
At another point in the interview, when asked what he knew about Huang’s other extramarital affairs, Trump reportedly said: “I really didn’t get into that. I got into the business of chips, much more than the business of sex.”
TechCrunch has reached out to the White House for comment.

title_en: You don't have to look at your Apple Watch to get the time
title_fa: You don't have to look at your Apple Watch to get the time
excerpt_en: Your Apple Watch has a way to share the time that even supports Morse Code. See which of its three modes makes sense for your daily routine.
excerpt_fa: Your Apple Watch has a way to share the time that even supports Morse Code. See which of its three modes makes sense for your daily routine.
content_en:
You don't have to look at your Apple Watch to get the time
You can keep track of the time without missing a beat, thanks to a discreet Apple Watch setting that comes in a few versions to suit your schedule.
One of the ironies of smartwatches is that for some people, telling the time is low on the list of priorities. You can always check your iPhone if you need to, and most of us spend hours every day in front of some form of clock, whether it's a PC or an old analog ticker hanging on the wall. It's actually features like fitness tracking and quick notification checks that elevate the best Apple Watches to must-haves.
One way or another, we need to know the time, and Apple Watches come with a variety of ways to communicate it. Something you may not have heard of, though, is the ability to get it via vibration. It's something Apple calls Taptic Time, a reference to the Taptic Engine that produces haptic feedback.
Here we're going to explain how to enable Taptic Time, how it works and, perhaps most importantly, why you'd want to bother. The short answer to the last item is that for some people, a visual check just isn't an option.
How to turn on and use Taptic Time on your Apple Watch
To enable Taptic Time, launch the Settings app on your Apple Watch. Next, select Clock, then Taptic Time. Toggle the feature on. At that point, you'll be presented with three options: Digits, Terse or Morse Code.
That last one should probably be avoided unless you're a 19th-century telegraph operator. Terse may not be much better, though. It uses long taps to indicate that five hours have passed since midnight, short taps for additional hours, then long taps again for quarter-hour increments. It's not hard to learn, but a 15-minute margin of error could mean the difference between catching your rideshare to the airport and having to rebook your flight.
The most precise and intuitive option is Digits. This uses long taps for tens and short taps for ones and applies that to both hours and minutes. For example, 10:09 would be one long tap, a pause, then nine short taps.
When VoiceOver is on, you can also turn on Taptic Time by double-tapping the watch face while the screen is inactive. Apple notes, though, that Taptic Time won't work in any fashion if your Apple Watch is set to always speak the time. To fix that, you can go to Settings > Clock, then turn on Control With Silent Mode under Speak Time.
Who should actually use Taptic Time on an Apple Watch?
The honest answer is that most people shouldn't. Even if it's just every 15 minutes, having your wrist vibrate repeatedly can be annoying, much less trying to interpret a coded pattern. That's particularly true on recent Apple Watches, which have motors strong enough that alerts can be startling, even when you're expecting them.
The main beneficiaries of Taptic Time are going to be the visually impaired. In that scenario, it might initially seem strange to buy one of the best smartwatches. But with the right accessibility options enabled, you don't need to see well to benefit from some of the Apple Watch's selling points, like fitness tracking, or controlling music and some of the best smart home accessories without having your iPhone nearby.
If your eyesight is fine, you might nevertheless want haptic feedback to keep you more mindful of the time, in which case Terse mode will be the least intrusive choice. It's also conceivable that your job or hobbies might put you in situations where checking your wrist is impractical. I like to ride electric unicycles, for example — while that keeps my hands free, sometimes I need to focus on carving the pavement.

content_en:
Gone are the days when you could just buy your father a random tie or some leather-clad alcohol vessel or a shaving kit. Dads want — nay, deserve — something memorable. Luckily for you, it’s not that hard to find something special that he’ll approve of, and we’re here to guide you.
The Verge’s 2026 gift guide for dads
This year, why not get Dad a gift or two he won’t expect?
This year, why not get Dad a gift or two he won’t expect?
We’ve curated this year’s gift list with the modern father in mind, whether he’s a gamer, creator, chef, or simply a gadget lover. There’s a lot in here we think he’ll like, from noise-canceling headphones like the Sonos Ace Ultra and an autonomous drone to a brilliant QD-OLED monitor and a nifty light that’s perfect for illuminating his next campsite. Whatever your dad is into, we’ve got you covered.
Dyson PencilVac Fluffycones
Cleaning gadgets like Dyson’s PencilVac FluffyCones are never cheap, but they’re often worth the cost and a pleasure to use. The lightweight, broom-replacing stick vacuum doesn’t do carpets, but its rolling bars pack incredible cleaning power for touching up hard floors, including stairs.
Give the gift that fixes past home improvement transgressions. These handy Japanese-made pliers from Vampire Tools have one fundamental purpose — to remove stripped screws — and they’re damn good at it. The best part? Watching Dad’s face light up seconds before he sprints to the garage for them.
Peak Design City Backpack (15L)
Who would have thought a simple hook could make roaming the city with a backpack so much more convenient? After testing Peak Design’s well-designed bags, we’re convinced the clever addition is a game-changer for anyone who doesn’t want to leave their bag on the filthy ground.
Sharge Disk Pro 2 SSD / HDMI dock
Give your father a little nostalgia and a lot of convenience in one package with this stylish USB-C dock and SSD combo gadget. The cassette-shaped Sharge Disk Pro 2 works as a hub with support for HDMI at 4K, SD and microSD card slots, USB-A and USB-C ports, along with up to 8TB of storage stored within.
It’s time to help Dad ditch his collection of plastic reusable cups, which have clearly seen better days. NotNeutral’s hand-pressed, timeless tumbler offers ’70s vibes with a modern twist, making it the perfect vessel for whatever Dad twists into his favorite drink.
Belkin Wireless HDMI Display Adapter
For those who love travel but hate the constraints of a hotel TV, Belkin’s ConnectAir is a slick solution. Plug the transmitter into any device with a USB-C video-out port and the receiver into the TV’s HDMI port, and voilà, you’re easily (and wirelessly) connected.
Have you broken something fragile that seems impossible to mend? Maybe all you need is a Kintsugi Repair Kit, which provides the Japanese method and a special lacquer to repair and restore broken ceramics to good health. The resulting golden scar is merely to remind us that rebuilding is possible.
Werewolf’s affordable dongle kit provides an almost magical way to power nearly any DC device from a USB-C charger or portable battery. Program it from a mobile app, connect it to your old gear, and everything from a PC monitor to an original Game Boy can accept USB-C charging.
Nomad Stratos Band
If your father already owns an Apple Watch, the Nomad Stratos is a foolproof upgrade idea. The refined watch band features titanium links with a rubbery interior for durable comfort, and it comes in an array of subtle color options that make it as suitable for the office as it is for the slopes.
If you’re after a cheap, useful stocking stuffer, Trond’s reliable three-prong extension cord is a practical pick that’s available in leftward or rightward configurations to fit nearly any outlet. Dad will probably say, “Oh, I’ve always wanted one of these,” and this time he’ll mean it.
Camp Snap CS-Pro
The CS-Pro will make your dad feel like a private eye in the early ’80s. The retro-inspired digital camera serves up 16-megapixel stills and offers four filters accessible from its tactile dial, plus USB-C charging, a high-quality Xenon flash, and a 4GB SD card for plenty of vintage photo fun.
Antigravity A1 drone
Antigravity’s A1 is the ultimate gadget for the dad who dreams of owning the sky. The compact drone comes with specialized goggles that will make him feel like he’s in the cockpit, and it records always-on, 360-degree 8K video. It’s an exhilarating flight experience and an excellent creator’s tool in one slick package.
Sonos Ace Ultra
Sonos raised its headphones game on all fronts with the Ace Ultra, which deliver better noise canceling, improved sound, and the feature we’ve all been waiting for: Wi-Fi support. With the ability to bounce audio across your Sonos ecosystem, including from a TV via newer Sonos soundbars, Dad’s sonic sanctuary is finally complete.
WiiM’s first soundbar builds on its seamless Sonos-esque connectivity with a sleek design, detailed sound, and up-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos spatial audio. It also pairs with other speakers for surround sound through a no-fuss setup process, including ones you already own that are linked to one of WiiM’s amplifiers.
Alienware AW3426DW QD-OLED Gaming Monitor
Your dad needs an awesome monitor, but there are 10 billion options. Alienware’s 34-inch Penta Tandem QD-OLED delivers top-end picture quality, with vibrant colors and perfect blacks, plus a swift 280Hz refresh rate. Best of all, it’s not nearly as expensive as you might think.
If your dad is still reading books on his phone (or aging e-reader), it’s time for an upgrade. The latest in Amazon’s series of waterproof, auto-dimming e-readers loads books faster than the prior model and offers a slick aluminum upgrade. No matter which you choose, it’s a better way to bring the library along.

title_en: The battery in your Fitbit Edge is replaceable, but it's not as easy as you'd think
title_fa: The battery in your Fitbit Edge is replaceable, but it's not as easy as you'd think
excerpt_en: Google partnered with iFixit for a step-by-step guide to replacing the Fitbit Edge's battery.
excerpt_fa: Google partnered with iFixit for a step-by-step guide to replacing the Fitbit Edge's battery.
content_en:
The battery in your Fitbit Edge is replaceable, but it's not as easy as you'd think
You can get a manual from iFixit for free to guide you through the process.
After a brief period of people worrying that Google that was abandoning Fitbit devices in favor of the Pixel Watch, the company recently assuaged those fears by releasing two new devices, led by the Fitbit Edge. It's an obvious successor to the Charge series, albeit without Google Pay, or EDA scans for measuring stress.
An enhancement that might've caught your attention is the product's user-replaceable battery. The dirty secret of most fitness trackers (and smartwatches, for that matter) is that while they can last for years, if their batteries aren't replaced, their capacity will inevitably shrink until it becomes unusable. In theory, as long Google maintains app support and compatible batteries are still in warehouses, an Edge can last indefinitely.
This isn't quite like replacing the AAs in a flashlight, however, or even the coin battery you might find in an analog watch. You need specialized gear, and the process is delicate enough that there's a risk of sabotaging your Fitbit if you make a mistake.
What makes the Fitbit Edge battery replacement so complicated
Google's partner on this is iFixit, which provides a free PDF manual once you've signed into their website. Before you begin, however, you need to buy specialized parts and tools, including not just a fresh battery, but replacement screws for the surrounding equipment. That might seem strange, but iFixit says that these replacement parts can only be used once, a claim which may or may not say anything about the original parts as well.
Where things get risky is after you've managed to pry open the Edge's case. Its O-ring can fall out, and you'll need to reassemble that if you want your device to retain any water resistance. You'll also need a pair of tweezers, and needless to say, poking circuits could accidentally break something, as could static shock. iFixit recommends precautions like a grounding mat, and even avoiding any clothing that could build up a static charge, such as fleece.
For some owners, the major hurdle is going to be the scale of the operation. The screws and connectors involved are tiny, even by the standards of most electronics. If your hands aren't steady, this process could prove frustrating or outright impossible, speaking as someone who's hand-assembled desktop PCs.
Are there any alternatives to Google's procedure?
Officially, no. If you don't want to perform the procedure yourself, Google doesn't offer a paid replacement service. The company might conceivably perform a free swap if you've got a defective battery and you're still under warranty, but you're otherwise expected to handle things yourself. If you do qualify for a battery fix, there's a chance that Google will simply send you a replacement Edge.
As time goes on, third-party options might arrive, yet Google cautions against using unofficial parts, stating that "a non-qualified battery and improper disposal may present a risk of fire, explosion, leakage, and/or other hazards." The company is, of course, covering itself legally — but there's a grain of truth in that there's no telling what the quality of a generic part may be. Lithium-ion batteries can burst into flames if they're damaged or defective. Even with Google's official parts, you should be prepared to dispose of a battery in a fireproof container.
All this helps to explain why more wearables haven't gone the replaceable route. Companies don't want to be on the hook for their customers' mistakes, and it remains to be seen how many people will actually take advantage of the option. By the time an Edge's battery wears out, you might be more inclined to buy a newer device than resuscitate last-gen hardware.

content_en:
The US Army is moving ahead with plans to detonate the nation’s stockpile of lead azide at an ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa, at approximately 9:00AM CST on Wednesday. The Verge reached out to experts on what to expect, and will keep this post updated.
Why the US Army is about to blow up nearly 10,000 pounds of unstable explosives in Iowa
The US Army is scrambling to contain any potential lead pollution that could spread if an old stockpile of explosives blows up.
The US Army is scrambling to contain any potential lead pollution that could spread if an old stockpile of explosives blows up.
What material is the Army planning to detonate?
There are 68 drums holding about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, an unstable chemical compound created to detonate munitions like grenades. The US started using lead azide as a primary explosive almost a century ago before “moving away” from it about 15 years ago because of how difficult the material is to store and transport, Robert Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), said in a Tuesday press briefing. At that point, the US transferred its remaining stockpile of lead azide to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. Lead azide will explode at 350 degrees Celsius (662F). But it is also sensitive to flame, friction, or sudden shock, including fluctuations in temperature.
Some of the material on site in Iowa is more than 60 years old. The material can crystallize as it degrades over time, becoming unstable enough to explode even at ambient temperatures. The Army noted some deterioration of the material in 2009 — but not any “dangerous crystallization” at the time, according to Cekada.
“It’s not a matter of if, it’s a matter of when.”
The chemical was stored in liquid form, embedded in sawdust and burlap bags inside the drums. Water and ethanol were also added to the containers to keep the lead azide from freezing in the winter. But during a March inspection, Cekada said ATF noticed “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels.” That made the material too unstable for them to open the barrels to add more water and ethanol, Cekada said. Removing a lid might cause the barrels to detonate.
Why is the Army detonating it now?
Officials have been trying to figure out what to do with the crystallized lead azide since that alarming March inspection. The Army initially hired a contractor to safely dissolve the chemicals but canceled the contract earlier this year, according to reporting by The New York Times. Using a chemical neutralization agent “proved to be an unsafe method,” Army Col. Aaron Teller, commander of the 71st Explosive Ordinance Disposal Group, said at the Tuesday briefing, because crystallization on the outside of the barrels made it too risky to open the lids.
“Everyone that we’ve spoken to through their experience has determined that this is the only safe path forward,“ Cekada said at the briefing. If they leave the chemicals as is, he said, they’re still at risk of exploding. “It’s not a matter of if, it’s a matter of when.”
What are the risks?
Compared to an uncontrolled, spontaneous explosion, a controlled detonation is supposed to limit the amount of lead dust unleashed on surrounding communities and the environment. Still, the dust plume could reach as far as 100 miles away from the site. The Army has released maps showing where lead dust is expected to travel based on its modeling.
The last time the Army disposed of lead azide this way at a comparable scale was in 1977, according to Teller. At the time, they detonated 7,000 pounds of the material in Colorado in open air “with zero mitigation.” Even then, 75 percent of the lead particulate stayed on site, Teller said at the briefing. The Army now believes it can “significantly reduce” the spread of that last 25 percent of lead using walls made up of four 16,000-gallon water tanks to capture lead particulate and hopefully prevent it from escaping into the atmosphere.
The 80-year-old earth-covered magazines holding the lead azide are cracked and deteriorating, Teller noted, and they are likely to break open after the detonation. To prepare, they’ve covered it with tarp and a special containment screen for lead. They also plan to flood it with 2 feet of foam to capture particulate pollution. Adam Telle, Acting Secretary of the Army, also said the Army has set out “state of the art gel blocks in huge quantities all around to ensure that we absorb as much of this blast as we possibly can.”
There is no “safe” level of exposure to lead
Last week, the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club sought a court order to stop the explosion from taking place, pending an Environmental and Health Impact Statement and an investigation into alternatives to detonating the material. President Donald Trump chimed in on social media, calling for a pause until a federal appeals court gave the Army the green light after previously granting a temporary stay. The court on Monday denied the emergency motion to stop the explosion, clearing the way for the Army to move forward.
What precautions can people nearby take?
The Iowa Department of Health and Human Services (Iowa HHS) recommends that anyone in potentially affected areas stay indoors and keep windows shut for 24 to 48 hours after the detonation. Iowa HHS also suggests switching off HVAC systems that might bring outdoor air inside or set them to modes that recirculate air, and using an air purifier with a HEPA filter.
FEMA is helping relocate Middletown residents and others within a voluntary 5-mile evacuation zone. People who are pregnant, children, and individuals with chronic diseases should evacuate the affected areas, Sean Kaufman, principal deputy assistant secretary for preparedness and response at the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response, said at the briefing. “Outside of that area, if you’re close to that proximity and you’re uncomfortable, I think you need to do what...

title_en: Australia to pass safety bill that could result in massive fines for tech platforms
title_fa: Australia to pass safety bill that could result in massive fines for tech platforms
excerpt_en: Australian lawmakers are close to passing the Digital Duty of Care Bill, an amendment to the country's Online Safety Act of 2021.
excerpt_fa: Australian lawmakers are close to passing the Digital Duty of Care Bill, an amendment to the country's Online Safety Act of 2021.
content_en:
Australia to pass safety bill that could result in massive fines for tech platforms
The amendment would give the country a similar ability to fine tech companies as the EU’s Digital Services Act from 2022.
Australian lawmakers are close to passing the Digital Duty of Care Bill, the Associated Press reports, an amendment to the country's Online Safety Act of 2021 that would set minimum safety standards for online platforms and provide ways to fine tech companies that don't comply. The bill follows Australia's recent social media ban for children under 16, an attempt to protect younger internet users with limited success so far.
If passed, the Digital Duty of Care Bill would require online platforms and services like games, social media apps and AI chatbots to protect Australians from harmful content and conduct, according to the AP, including protecting children from exposure to content that promotes eating disorders and pornography. It would also guarantee users the ability to opt out of algorithmic feeds and empower the country's eSafety Commissioner to remove "nudify" websites and apps that use AI to generate and spread nonconsensual nude images. As with the European Union's Digital Services Act, the bill's real teeth come from its possible fines. In this case, Australian regulators could fine tech companies up to five percent of their global revenue, a cap that was raised this week from 109 million AUD, or about $72 million in the US, to help the bill pass the Senate.
"Vaguely defined 'harms,' backed by penalties of up to 5% of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech," US Ambassador to Australia David Brat posted on X. "As Australia's largest foreign investor, the US is concerned with regulations that impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors."
Similar concerns have been raised about the UK's Online Safety Act, which also applies safety standards to online platforms, and helped encourage a wave of new age verification systems across US apps and services in the last year. The Wikimedia Foundation, the owner of Wikipedia, has challenged the ways the UK's law categorizes platforms as one example of how these laws can be ill-defined or overly broad. Australia's bill is expected to clear Parliament and become law by the end of the week, according to the AP.

title_en: Improve your Starlink Wi-Fi speed with this app setting
title_fa: Improve your Starlink Wi-Fi speed with this app setting
excerpt_en: See how a single setting in the Starlink app can improve your home internet speed, and figure out whether switching it on makes sense for your setup.
excerpt_fa: See how a single setting in the Starlink app can improve your home internet speed, and figure out whether switching it on makes sense for your setup.
content_en:
Improve your Starlink Wi-Fi speed with this app setting
Is your Starlink Wi-Fi slower than it should be? A simple change in the app can help, though it comes with a few trade-offs worth knowing first.
While Starlink has had a lot of bad press in 2026 — mostly because of reported slowdowns in Ukraine and its general association with Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk — there's no denying that for some people, it may be their best or only internet option. That's because Starlink satellites have wide global coverage, reaching areas inaccessible not just to landline connections but potentially competing cellular and satellite services as well.
There are a variety of ways Starlink can be optimized, an obvious one being dish placement. Less obvious, though, is controlling how your system broadcasts Wi-Fi. You'd think the hard part would be capturing signals from space, after all, not bouncing them a few more feet to your laptop or TV.
What we're specifically talking about here is splitting your Wi-Fi into separate 2.4 and 5GHz networks in the Starlink app. We'll explain what that means, why it can be beneficial and when you may want to stick with the normal unified setting.
Why splitting your Starlink Wi-Fi might provide a speed boost
If you already know why you'd want to split Wi-Fi, let's cut to the chase. All you have to do is find and select the Add Network option, then toggle Split Network. You'll be asked to name the two new networks, which should probably include "2.4" and "5" so you can tell which network your devices are connecting to.
For everyone else, it helps to know that most Wi-Fi routers are dual-band, broadcasting over two main frequency bands, 2.4 and 5GHz. Starlink's bundled hardware doesn't currently support the newer 6GHz band, even when it's equipped with Wi-Fi 7. The reason a split might help is that 5GHz is inherently faster than 2.4GHz. Shorter wavelengths translate not just into higher potential speeds but more non-overlapping channels. Overlap can result in congestion and interference. For devices that support 5GHz, then, forcing them to use the band all the time may result in noticeable speed boosts. As with any Wi-Fi network, exact performance figures are going to depend on a variety of factors, including not just your router but the range and kinds of devices connecting to your network.
As if that weren't enough, some low-power devices, such as many Wi-Fi smart LED light bulbs, are 2.4GHz-only. If they're competing with devices that could be on 5GHz, they might be encountering unnecessary congestion of their own.
When splitting your Starlink Wi-Fi can cause problems
The first potential issue here is range. The 2.4GHz band offers the greatest reach of any Wi-Fi band, typically up to 150 feet (45 meters) indoors, versus 5GHz's 50 to 75 feet (15 to 25 meters). It also offers better penetration through walls and other obstacles. In some scenarios, then, limiting devices to 5GHz may result in a flaky signal or none at all where things were previously stable. Under a unified network, devices can flip between bands automatically as needed.
The other major concern is that devices on one network ID might not be able to talk to those on the other. They should be able to on paper, and naturally, that won't matter if all they have to do is communicate with the internet. But if you do encounter this issue, it can wreak havoc, particularly with a mix of smart home accessories that require specific bands. You may not be able to configure them all to work together, let alone trigger complex automations.
One final problem is convenience. Reassigning a bunch of devices to new networks can be a hassle, and to deal with range, you may have to manually switch some mobile devices every time you take them into a particular room. If you're not encountering any performance barriers with your existing setup, you might want to leave Starlink untouched.

But if you do encounter this issue, it can wreak havoc, particularly with a mix of smart home accessories that require specific bands. You may not be able to configure them all to work together, let alone trigger complex automations.
One final problem is convenience. Reassigning a bunch of devices to new networks can be a hassle, and to deal with range, you may have to manually switch some mobile devices every time you take them into a particular room. If you're not encountering any performance barriers with your existing setup, you might want to leave Starlink untouched.

title_en: Huawei is guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, US jury rules
title_fa: Huawei is guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, US jury rules
excerpt_en: The charges against the Chinese tech company date back to 2019.
excerpt_fa: The charges against the Chinese tech company date back to 2019.
content_en:
Huawei is guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, US jury rules
The company is already barred from US sales, but the verdict could cost it billions in penalties.
Huawei Technologies has been found guilty of bank fraud and conspiracy to steal trade secrets by a US jury, the Associated Press reports. The verdict is the result of charges brought by the Department of Justice in 2019, though the jury acquitted Huawei of racketeering conspiracy, as well as conspiracy to obstruct justice.
Racketeering is traditionally reserved for organized criminal acts — the kind often associated with the Mafia, for example — but the AP writes US prosecutors thought the charge could apply to what they described as Huawei's repeated theft of intellectual property and trade secrets. The company has been accused of copying or outright stealing from competitors in the past, and the DOJ pointed to Huawei's sale of routers with code copied from a competitor as evidence. Prosecutors also accused Huawei of violating US sanctions by selling equipment to Iran and North Korea, and misleading banks and officials to hide it.
In a statement, Huawei welcomed its acquittal on the racketeering charge, saying it lacked "factual basis."
"We believe the government's remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit," the company continued. "The five trade secret-related disputes cited by the government were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades. No court ever found Huawei liable for willful intellectual property misappropriation, and the company was never ordered to pay damages for trade secret misappropriation. We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests." Huawei attorney Brian Heberlig told AP the company planned to appeal its convictions.
Huawei isn't allowed to sell its products in the US due to its placement on the Federal Communications Commission's Covered List, so outside of the possibility of paying "billions of dollars in penalties," per the AP, it's not clear how these charges will impact its business. In 2025, the FCC opened an investigation into whether Huawei and fellow Chinese companies ZTE and China Telecom were circumventing those restrictions, so the company could face even more scrutiny in the US soon.

title_en: Jensen Huang still thinks a succession plan creates unnecessary hierarchy
title_fa: Jensen Huang still thinks a succession plan creates unnecessary hierarchy
excerpt_en: It's a remarkable stance for a company that spent the last two weeks finding out what happens without its founder.
excerpt_fa: It's a remarkable stance for a company that spent the last two weeks finding out what happens without its founder.
content_en:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang kicked off his return to the chipmaker he co-founded by holding an all-hands meeting that covered remorse, therapy, and even the company’s code of conduct, according to accounts from multiple insiders who spoke to the media.
The topic of succession planning also came up — a particularly sticky issue seen as a key risk at Nvidia. Huang reportedly told staff that Nvidia doesn’t require succession planning because of its unique business model, CNBC reported, citing an unnamed source who was present. Surprisingly, given the events of the last two weeks, Huang argued that a succession plan would create unnecessary hierarchy.
Investors and analysts saw the issue differently earlier this month, when Huang resigned as CEO following his admission that he had extramarital affairs with at least two people, including one whom the U.S. government suspects of being a Chinese spy.
Nvidia is a flat organization, unlike other large corporations that have a swath of C-suite executives and multiple layers of management. Huang sits at the top and says he has about 60 direct reports. Nvidia has just five executive officers running the show, including Huang. The other four are CFO Colette Kress, who was interim CEO for 12 days; Ajay Puri, who heads worldwide field operations; Debora Shoquist, executive vice president of operations; and Timothy Teter, executive vice president and general counsel, according to the company’s regulatory filings.
Huang has previously defended the company’s structure in numerous interviews, including one in March with podcaster Lex Fridman.
“When you’re designing a company, you should first think about what is it that you want the company to produce,” Huang said in the interview. “You know, I see a lot of companies’ organization charts, and they all look the same. Hamburger [company] organization charts, software organization charts, and car company organization charts. They all look the same. And it doesn’t make any sense to me. You know, the goal of company is to be the machinery, the mechanism, the system that produces the output. And that output is the product that we like to create.”
Huang’s comments to staff, and his previous remarks on the topic of succession, may not be enough to assuage the board or shareholders over the long term, however.

title_en: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets
title_fa: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets
excerpt_en: A jury has found Huawei guilty of stealing US trade secrets, as reported earlier by NBC News and Bloomberg. The verdict, handed down in a federal court in New York, concludes a years-long legal battle that accused the Chinese telecom giant of stealing source code and proprietary...
excerpt_fa: A jury has found Huawei guilty of stealing US trade secrets, as reported earlier by NBC News and Bloomberg. The verdict, handed down in a federal court in New York, concludes a years-long legal battle that accused the Chinese telecom giant of stealing source code and proprietary...
content_en:
A jury has found Huawei guilty of stealing US trade secrets, as reported earlier by NBC News and Bloomberg. The verdict, handed down in a federal court in New York, concludes a years-long legal battle that accused the Chinese telecom giant of stealing source code and proprietary technology from several companies, including T-Mobile, Cisco, and Motorola.
Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets
The Chinese telecom giant was also found guilty of bank fraud.
The Chinese telecom giant was also found guilty of bank fraud.
The Department of Justice’s 2018 criminal indictment against Huawei came to light following the arrest of the company’s CFO, Wanzhou Meng, whom the agency accused of fraud. Though the indictment against Meng was eventually dismissed, she admitted to misleading banks over Huawei’s operations in Iran as part of a deferred prosecution agreement. The US government blacklisted Huawei in 2019 over national security concerns.
In total, the jury found Huawei guilty of 10 of 12 criminal counts, including money laundering, violating US sanctions, bank fraud, wire fraud, and conspiracy to defraud the US. The company was acquitted of engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice. Huawei’s sentencing is set for September 14th, 2027, where it may face “financial penalties including criminal fines, forfeiture, and restitution,” according to the DOJ.
“For over two decades, Huawei built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft, and deception,” Tysen A. Duva, the assistant attorney general of the DOJ’s criminal division, says in a statement. “Huawei’s crimes threatened the U.S. financial system, took advantage of American companies that compete honestly in the global telecommunications market, and undermined our national security.”
In a statement to NBC News, a Huawei spokesperson said the charges are “without legal or factual merit” and that it plans to appeal the decision. Huawei didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

title_en: In all-hands meeting, Jensen Huang thanks White House and says he’s in therapy
title_fa: In all-hands meeting, Jensen Huang thanks White House and says he’s in therapy
excerpt_en: The Nvidia founder apologized to his staff on Tuesday and said he was grateful for a second chance to lead the company.
excerpt_fa: The Nvidia founder apologized to his staff on Tuesday and said he was grateful for a second chance to lead the company.
content_en:
After a whirlwind period during which Jensen Huang’s life fell apart and then came back together again, the Nvidia founder now wants his staff to know that he’s a changed man.
Huang held Nvidia’s first all-hands meeting on Tuesday since his reinstatement on Monday. During that meeting, CNBC reported that Huang struck a “remorseful tone” and told the crowd “I hurt all of you.”
The founder, whose extramarital affairs have been accused of jeopardizing everything from the stock market to U.S. national security, went on to describe how difficult the current moment is for him: “This is going to be the hardest company meeting I’ve ever done, and the second hardest meeting I have ever done,” Huang reportedly told staff.
“The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife,” he added.
The CEO admitted in the meeting that he had flouted Nvidia’s code of conduct, which he himself had largely devised. Huang emphasized that the code of conduct was still in effect, but that mitigating circumstances would matter a lot. As Wired reported Huang’s statement, it “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door.”
Huang told staff that he’s in therapy and also said that he was grateful for a second chance at the company.
The CEO is now walking a difficult tight rope between reasserting his authority over one of the world’s most powerful and influential companies, and conceding that he may have made some mistakes. He also tackled the difficult question of President Trump’s role in his restoration. The president reportedly called Nvidia’s board directly to lobby for Huang’s return, but in his talk, Huang downplayed Trump’s role
Huang thanked the administration on Tuesday for “providing Nvidia with quick access to intelligence that he said helped the board determine that the national security risks the company faced in reinstating him were low,” The Wall Street Journal writes.
Huang will likely need the administration’s support as he weathers an upcoming wave of congressional scrutiny from a newly Democrat-led government. The CEO is scheduled to appear for a public Senate Banking Committee hearing next week and, in the coming weeks, he will be called to appear for a number of different closed House hearings, including for the Intelligence Committee, the Foreign Affairs Committee, and the China Select Committee.

excerpt_en: Game modding communities are racing to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC, but one big effort has been taken down by Take-Two today. Leonida, a fan project by 15-year-old "NotRexed," has vanished after a DMCA takedown notice from GTA VI publisher Take-Two. Leonida was...
excerpt_fa: Game modding communities are racing to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC, but one big effort has been taken down by Take-Two today. Leonida, a fan project by 15-year-old "NotRexed," has vanished after a DMCA takedown notice from GTA VI publisher Take-Two. Leonida was...
content_en:
Game modding communities are racing to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC, but one big effort has been taken down by Take-Two today. Leonida, a fan project by 15-year-old “NotRexed,” has vanished after a DMCA takedown notice from GTA VI publisher Take-Two.
GTA VI PC recompilation project shut down by Take-Two
Modders are racing to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC.
Modders are racing to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC.
Leonida was designed to translate a leaked GTA VI Xbox build to run natively on Windows. Cyberleek, the leaker who posted multiple GTA VI gameplay videos over the summer, published a full Xbox build of the game earlier this week. The leak has kicked recompilation efforts up a notch, as modders race to reverse-engineer the game’s code and rebuild it into native PC code.
Some have managed to get the game to boot on PC, but recompiling the full game won’t be easy — even with help from AI tools like Claude. Take-Two is trying to slow this progress, and its IP enforcement team targeted the main GitHub repository for Leonida and more than 2,900 forks of it, claiming that it “infringes upon Take-Two’s copyrighted works and facilitates copyright infringement of Rockstar Games title, Grand Theft Auto VI.”
PortWatch VI is tracking the efforts to recompile, emulate, or port the leaked Xbox build over to PC. At the time of publishing, the VIctory project and forks of it are leading the way. People are also trying to use XCL, a compatibility layer that runs Xbox Series X games on a Windows PC, to get GTA VI running.
At this point, it seems like Take-Two might not be able to avoid the inevitable here. The clock started ticking down to the release of the PC version last week, and if recent reports are true, we might see it in a few months. If GTA VI is close to being officially ready for PC, we could hear about a release before modders manage to get the game running on PC unofficially.

title_en: Even the best AI agents struggle with everyday life
title_fa: Even the best AI agents struggle with everyday life
excerpt_en: As millions embrace personal AI assistants, a new benchmark reveals that even the most advanced AI models struggle to complete everyday tasks reliably and safely without introducing potential new problems.
excerpt_fa: As millions embrace personal AI assistants, a new benchmark reveals that even the most advanced AI models struggle to complete everyday tasks reliably and safely without introducing potential new problems.
content_en:
AI companies have spent the last couple of months marketing personal AI agents as tools to take over the digital drudgery of human existence — and millions have been sold on the vision, handing over their shopping schedules, travel plans, and everyday responsibilities to AI assistants. But new research suggests that even the most advanced AI models struggle to reliably and safely navigate the messy details of people’s lives.
According to ShellBench, a new benchmark for everyday agent work, even the most advanced models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta failed more than a third of the time. Across all models tested, 15.7% of attempts failed at least one safety requirement, often leading to unintended consequences.
ShellBench was developed in collaboration with researchers at The OpenClaw Foundation, Parsewave, Hugging Face, Red Hat, and UC Berkeley, drawing on more than 10 million anonymized, real-world AI agent interactions to see how agents perform on the everyday work people actually delegate to them.
The research comes as personal AI assistants are finding new popularity among developers, with Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic all fighting for a piece of the market with Muse, Dots, and Claude Duet, respectively.
In October, Meta said more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada had set up its personal AI agent, Muse, within six weeks of launch, with about a quarter using it daily. That number is expected to grow as Meta implants Muse directly into Instagram DMs. Despite growing popularity among consumers, we still have little evidence about how reliable AI personal assistant products actually are.
ShellBench suggests that the unreliable nature of most everyday data sources still causes problems for many state-of-the-art systems. A successful agent should be able to navigate messy personal workspaces containing emails, calendar entries, spreadsheets, receipts, chat logs, outdated information, and phishing attempts, and figure out which information is relevant, what is private, and how to deliver the requested outcome without creating new problems.
It seems many of today’s AI agents are still not up to the task. Not only did even the highest-performing agents frequently fail to meet the requirements of a task, but they also lacked consistency. When researchers ran each task three times under identical conditions, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, the highest-scoring model, nailed all three attempts less than half the time.
For autonomous assistants that are meant to run in the background without supervision, it’s a problem if users need to run an agent multiple times to get a result they trust.
Additionally, about 10% of otherwise correct attempts failed at least one safety criterion. Across the models and harnesses tested, agents failed to, for example, adequately account for a child’s school pickup 79.5% of the time. When handling laptop custody records, agents failed a requirement to identify and withhold a sensitive bank upload token in 18.6% of attempts. In another task, agents recommended duplicate or incorrect invoice payments 40.3% of the time.
The findings highlight a major issue for users adopting consumer personal AI assistants, namely that there’s always a risk that an agent can create more headaches in the course of trying to fulfill an otherwise ordinary request.
While AI benchmarks have largely focused on coding, professional work, or testing on specific tasks, ShellBench is attempting to evaluate how models perform on multi-step personal tasks within different agent harnesses — the software that controls how a model accesses information, uses tools, and takes actions.
While the researchers found model choice had a greater overall impact on performance than harness choice, among the more capable models, AI agent performance became more dependent on the harness.
For example, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra outperformed Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 when operating within the Pi harness, but it performed worse when both models were tested within Claude Code.
Meta’s Muse Wonder Full scored 56% in Pi, but only 38.1% in Claude Code. Meta’s Muse Wonder 1.0, meanwhile, averaged a success rate of 39.7% across the five harnesses tested.
Notably, while the researchers tested models from Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic, they didn’t evaluate them within the native harnesses of Muse, Dots, or Claude Duet, so the results may not be representative of the experience millions of consumers are having with the product today.
TechCrunch has reached out to Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, and the researchers in the study.

Notably, while the researchers tested models from Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic, they didn’t evaluate them within the native harnesses of Muse, Dots, or Claude Duet, so the results may not be representative of the experience millions of consumers are having with the product today.
TechCrunch has reached out to Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, and the researchers in the study.

title_en: Walmart teams up with Meta to bring Black Friday deals to AI agent Muse
title_fa: Walmart teams up with Meta to bring Black Friday deals to AI agent Muse
excerpt_en: Walmart now lets customers shop Black Friday deals through Muse, Meta’s AI agent.
excerpt_fa: Walmart now lets customers shop Black Friday deals through Muse, Meta’s AI agent.
content_en:
Shopping with AI is becoming less of a futuristic idea and more of something companies expect us to do. Walmart is the latest retailer making that shift, teaming up with Meta to let customers shop its Black Friday deals through Muse, Meta’s AI agent.
The partnership, announced Tuesday, gives shoppers another way to find products, compare prices, and make purchases without browsing Walmart’s website themselves. Instead, customers can simply tell Muse what they are looking for and let the AI do the work.
The announcement highlights how differently Walmart and Amazon are approaching AI shopping. While Amazon has taken steps to stop third-party AI agents from making purchases for customers, Walmart is leaning into the idea.
To get started, users open the Muse app, sign in to their Walmart account, and return to the assistant to begin shopping. They can ask it to find specific products, compare options, or track down deals. Once a customer makes a request in Muse, the assistant sends it to Walmart, which returns relevant products and helps build a shopping cart.
Walmart says it has built privacy protections into the experience. For instance, Muse doesn’t get access to a customer’s Walmart shopping history or other personal information. Shoppers can also set spending limits, require approval before purchases, and review orders placed by the agent.
Plus, the company notes users can always delete their agent’s profile if they want to.
The experience is powered by Walmart’s Agent Gateway, a new system that allows outside AI assistants to connect directly with the retailer’s online store. This launched in October, and the company is planning to open it up to more developers and AI platforms, meaning Muse could eventually be just one of several assistants capable of shopping Walmart’s online store.
Walmart is not the only company teaming up with Meta’s Muse. Instacart also recently joined forces with the AI assistant.
Beyond Muse, Walmart has recently rolled out more AI-powered features to its own shopping assistant, Sparky.
Some of the newer additions include turning handwritten shopping lists into shopping carts, using photos and voice commands to find products, and helping customers get around their local store. Shoppers can search for an item and use a pin on the store map to see exactly which aisle it’s in. There’s also a “Flash Price Tag” button that makes the item’s shelf label light up.
